record.file_problem: Figures are referenced but their numerical values are not available in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The post uses SAEs as a tool for decomposing model activations, framing them as a way to tackle superposition, but its experiments test SAE normalization rather than the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The post reports experiments on feature suppression, input-norm/L0 correlation, L1/L0 agreement, and reconstruction performance. These concern the effects of changing the SAE architecture and loss; they do not measure the claim versions. The eligible results here are the reported measurements of the learned feature dictionary's norms and cosine similarities.
record.test_reason: The post proposes an SAE architecture variant (NSAE) and reports its own method's performance (feature suppression ratio, L0/input-norm correlation, L1/L0 agreement, reconstruction score) against the standard SAE. It uses SAEs as a tool for superposition but does not test whether features are superposed, whether SAE features are interpretable or canonical units, or any toy-model geometry.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The author concludes that NSAE reduces feature suppression (||x'||/||x|| near 1), removes the positive relationship between layer mean input norm and L0, and makes L1 track L0 more closely. Reconstruction score is essentially unchanged, but L2 loss is slightly higher and convergence is slower. The correction/pillar/direction vector types are hypotheses left for future work.
record.recipe_differences: The proposed NSAE changes the activation to tanh(ReLU(We x + be + noise)), removes the decoder unit-norm constraint, and scales the L1 coefficient using the squared mean input norm per layer.
record.method_sensitivity: The author reports different outcomes across layers for baseline input-norm/L0 relationships and notes that results depend on the SAE architecture; the normalized group's L0 also varies with layer index.

fits_no_version.finding: The SAE architecture choice (unit-norm decoder vs. NSAE with tanh and norm-scaled L1) changes L0 across layers, feature suppression, and the dictionary's norm and cosine structure, while reconstruction score stays similar.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The properties of SAE dictionaries (sparsity level per layer, norms, near-duplicate directions) depend on architecture and loss normalization choices.

record.problems: The author describes the experiments as relatively small in scale due to compute limits. Figure values are not numerically reported in the supplied text, and the proposed interpretations of dictionary vector types are explicitly left for future investigation.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results omitted. The other experimental results concern SAE normalization effects rather than the claim versions.

untested.parts: All parts: no toy models, no sparsity-dependent phase transition, no geometry analysis.
All parts: no capacity or importance analysis.
All parts: SAEs are trained on GPT-2 MLP outputs, but feature recovery and interpretability are not evaluated, and features spread across neurons are not measured.
All parts: no completeness, stability across seeds, or canonicality test; the dictionary statistics compare architectures only.

record.verdict_notes: The three rows describe the study's own NSAE dictionary versus the standard SAE. They are method characterisation, not tests of any version. The study is small-scale: two runs per group on GPT-2 MLP outputs, with figure-only results and no uncertainty reported. Commenters note that comparisons are not L0-matched; the author added a layer-5 matched comparison.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, overcomplete sparse features, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry are not tested.
The post does not test capacity competition, feature importance, or dedicated versus shared dimensions.
It does not test non-capacity explanations for polysemantic neurons.
Although SAEs are trained on GPT2 activations, the post does not validate that the learned dictionary recovers sparse, interpretable model features or measure feature distribution across neurons.
Completeness, stability, and canonicality of SAE features are not tested.
The post does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features.
